utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning. I would like to greet the parties and all the members of our staff. Mr. Cayley, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Judge Riad, Judge Wald. Good morning learned counsel for the Defence. We're continuing today, Your Honour, with the cross-examination of Mr. Zeljko Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Shall we introduce him?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, the usher is just at this moment getting him from the witness room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have other witnesses today, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think the Defence have their third witness, but Mr. Petrusic may be able to be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Judge Riad, I think actually the wrong witness has been brought in. It's the gentleman with the moustache.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So we have another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We're moving through them very rapidly, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would like just to announce that we'll have to finish at a quarter to three because we have other functions. So I would hope we'll be through with the witnesses by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think Mr. Petrusic may have a few words.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. After Mr. Borovcanin, the Defence has another witness, and we expect to finish his examination-in-chief by the end of the working day, that is, by a quarter to three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We can call the right witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Borovcanin. Mr. Cayley will continue --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Realtime transcript read in error "JUDGE RODRIGUES: [Interpretation]"] -- asking questions now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if you recall, on Friday, I think we concluded where you confirmed to me that in July of 1995 Colonel Mirko Trivic was the commander of the 2nd Romanija Brigade. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade in 1995 was Mirko Trivic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall who the Chief of Staff of the Romanija Brigade was in July of 1995? Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, there is just a small confusion in the transcript before, that Judge Rodrigues is here. I want just to say that he is not here. "Judge Rodrigues," and even with "interpretation." He must have sent a message. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I see, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I'm right in saying that you were a member of the reconnaissance platoon of the 2nd Romanija Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1994 I joined the reconnaissance platoon and I remained a member of it until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And so in July of 1995 you were a member of the reconnaissance platoon?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said in your evidence that a man by the name of Bojovic was the commander of the reconnaissance platoon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the -- or leader of the reconnaissance platoon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you referred to him by two different first names. On one occasion you called him Milenko Bojovic and on another occasion you referred to him as Branko Bojovic. Do you remember what his first name was? Was it Milenko or Branko?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milenko Bojovic. I don't think I mentioned the name Branko.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, do you recall who the name of your battalion commander was?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battalion commander was Ljubo Eric.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Ljubo Eric was a major; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was a captain or a major. I'm not quite sure now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And what rank was Mr. Bojovic? Do you recall the commander of the reconnaissance platoon?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had the rank of corporal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall now -- I know it's a long time ago -- the names of any of the other battalion commanders within the Romanija Brigade, apart from Mr. Eric?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now I want you to think about the 9th of July again. And just to refresh your memory, you testified on Friday that by the evening of the 9th of July of 1995, you had reached the Alibegovac feature and the UN soldiers who were at the checkpoint nearby had actually surrendered to you and they had gone to Bratunac. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if the witness could be shown a map, which is Exhibit 829.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Borovcanin, I've produced a map of the area and highlighted a number of the places that you spoke about. If you could take a look at the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Judge Riad, would you mind and would Defence counsel mind if for just a moment I approached the witness, because this map is quite difficult to sort of come to terms with immediately and I wanted to help him where I've marked places on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do the Defence have any objection to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon, I wasn't really listening, so could you repeat your question, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, I have a map which, in fact, you gave to us and I've marked on it some of the locations that the witness spoke about and I just wanted to show him the places that I've marked so that he can become familiar with the map before I start asking him further questions, just to make his life a little bit easier. You can join me, if you want, at the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If necessary, and if the witness manages to find his way on the map, I'll join you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, do you see Kiprovo?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Alibegovac?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Brdo, Slapovici, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Suceska?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Jahorina?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Bojna?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Jasenovo, do you see that? Now, these two areas here marked in yellow are two UN checkpoints. Now, this one was called Kilo and this one was called Sierra?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'll return to the podium now. If I place this here on the ELMO, will you be all right to look at it? Can you see it clearly enough?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now, unfortunately, Your Honours, it doesn't come out very clearly. Do Your Honours have a copy of this map in front of you? You do; excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, could you point to the Alibegovac feature on this map.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, to the best of your recollection, you can see where Kiprovo is where I pointed it out to you. Which was the UN checkpoint which surrendered to your unit, was it Kilo or Sierra, K or S?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one here, next to Alibegovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So for the sake of the record, the witness has indicated that it was, in fact, checkpoint Kilo which was the checkpoint that his unit reached by the evening of the 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you stated in your evidence on Friday that you had been given strict orders not to shoot at the UN, not to seize sidearms or their equipment, and I think the agreement was that the troops be escorted to Bratunac. Are those three things correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my unit was there and, as far as I know, nothing was seized from them nor was any fire opened against the UN forces and they were escorted away.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, the Judges have, in fact, heard from one of the soldiers who was present at that particular checkpoint and he, indeed, confirms, as you stated, that not a shot was fired. Now, after the Dutch soldiers had surrendered, I think you moved forward to the old lines of the Bosnian army, you went to their trenches; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We only took over the trenches which earlier had been used by the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And how far were they from the UN checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it wasn't very far. A little hill up there. I can't remember exactly, maybe one kilometre, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you didn't actually see the UN soldiers taken away?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We took up these positions and there were other people who escorted them away.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you wouldn't know anything about whether or not these soldiers did, in fact, have their weapons taken away from them, their flak jackets, their blue helmets. You wouldn't know anything about that if that happened because you, in fact, were in the Bosnian army trenches?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no troops there. We all took up these positions. Surely five or six men couldn't have seized weapons and things.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But I'm right in saying that you, yourself, took no part in transferring the Dutch soldiers from the checkpoint to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you wouldn't be able to make any comment on the fact that the witness that the Judges heard stated that his weapon was taken away from him and that, in fact, all of the Dutch soldiers had their flak jackets removed and their blue helmets removed. You wouldn't know anything about that because you weren't, in fact, in Bratunac, were you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Your Honours, I just refer the Court to the testimony of Mr. Andere Stoelinga and the position at the transcript is 2275 where he speaks about these events. He was a soldier who testified before you who was, in fact, one of the soldiers at OP Kilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if we can move on in time, Mr. Borovcanin, and I want to now talk a little bit further about the 9th of July and the 11th of July. Now, you said in your evidence that, as far as you recall, there was no shelling when you reached the Alibegovac feature. You hadn't heard any shelling up until that point by the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said that along our route that we were moving, there was no need for shelling nor was there any shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the reasons for that, I think you said, was because the Muslim army had withdrawn, it had retreated?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, briefly, I want you to think about the 11th of July, and you said in your evidence that, on that particular day, you recall that there were air strikes by NATO aircraft against Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I'm correct in saying that I think you heard the explosions very clearly?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think the reason that you probably heard those explosions very clearly because, one, they were very loud and, two, the bombs were falling in a valley so the noise travelled right down the valley, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't falling in the valley. We were in the valley. They were above us, near the place where we had spent the night on the 10th in the evening. That is where the shells fell on that hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the Judges have heard evidence in this case, and Your Honours, I would refer to the UN report on Srebrenica which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 30, that two bombs were dropped by NATO forces, by NATO aircraft at 2.40 in the afternoon on the 11th of July. Do you recall hearing two explosions?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know now how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But nevertheless, it was very loud and you heard it. You heard a number of explosions.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard several explosions but I can't remember now how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I want you to think of the time period between the 6th of July and the 11th of July. What shelling did you hear during that period by your army, by the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a couple of explosions but, as I said, along our route, there was no shelling, but a couple of explosions could be heard from other directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you are aware, are you not, that there was very heavy shelling during that period, into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srebrenica was not shelled, as far as I am aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let me refresh your memory about this. Now, you may or may not be aware that present within the enclave during this period were not only Dutch UN forces but also a group of United Nations military observers whose task was to specifically monitor Bosnian Serb forces and shelling into the enclave. Were you aware of their presence?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, they were there and they produced a number of written reports, which the Judges have seen, over this period of time. And I will not show you all of the reports, they are in English, and I will read you small extracts and just ask for your comments on what they observed and/or heard over this period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So if I can have Exhibit 77/1. Judge Riad, I'm not going to go through -- these reports are voluminous; I'm just going to take extracts. I think Defence counsel have them if they wish to re-examine on them. If you could put the first page, paragraph 3, onto the ELMO. And this is a report from the 6th of July, Mr. Borovcanin, at 1735 hours. I'll read it to you. And this is a report from the period 3.30 in the morning on the 6th of July until 6.00 in the evening on that day. And this is what the UN military observers say: "Team Srebrenica reported a Bosnian Serb army offence launched and ongoing within the enclave as reported under separate cover. The Bosnian Serb army used tanks, artillery, mortars, rockets, and heavy machine-gun and have targeted the DutchBat headquarters and Bandera triangle, DutchBat observation posts Uniform and Sierra --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, could you read more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. "-- south of OP Hotel, Potocari township, Srebrenica township, and --" and then it gives a grid reference, 651849. "At least 250 artillery and mortar rounds have been recorded so far. The UNMO team have confirmed two fatalities and six casualties so far being taken to hospital. Further details re: casualties and shell investigations are not possible at this stage. DutchBat reported six 120-millimetre rockets landed close to their compound with only two exploding at about 3.30 hours Bravo on the 6th of July, 1995. The shelling of the surrounding area (Potocari) however continued until 1600 hours Bravo 6 July 1995, with two civilian casualties so far recorded." Now, Mr. Borovcanin, I'm not going to read any more of that. Did you hear any of that shelling and tank fire and rocket fire and heavy machine-gun fire on the 6th of July?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 6 of July I think we were between Jasenova and Kiprovo. I said that along our axis there was no shelling. I said that some explosions were heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you just put the map that you have in front of you and show the Judges where Kiprovo is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the camera could come out, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you point to Kiprovo, Mr. Borovcanin? And now point to Srebrenica. Now, each of those big squares on that map is a thousand metres, so during that period you were about 3.000 metres away from where these shells were falling and your evidence is that you heard very little in the way of explosions, heavy machine-gun fire, tank rounds exploding; you heard very little?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was shooting from machine-guns and automatic weapons, but shelling was rare.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's now move to the 7th of July. And if Prosecutor's Exhibit 77/3 could be placed on the ELMO, paragraph 3. This is a report, Your Honours, made at 1742 hours on the 7th of July. You can see the CapSat notation at the top of this exhibit when it was actually sent, I think, by satellite phone. And I'll read out what the UN military observers observed and heard on that day: "Team Srebrenica reported that the Bosnian Serb army continued their offensive on the enclave with heavy weapons since early this morning. DutchBat reported heavy shelling around their compound in Potocari, and as a result, three men were injured and brought by MSF, Medecins Sans Frontieres, to the hospital. UNMOs confirm this. At 1000 hours, unconfirmed reports indicated that the Bosnian Serb army are regrouping around former OP Echo, Company Hill, and Bratunac. At 1000 hours, two shells landed in Srebrenica village, but no one was wounded. At 1100 hours, four shells landed in Potocari, no injuries. At 1500 hours, three shells landed in Srebrenica and injured two men. One was picked up by our patrol and the other one by Medecins Sans Frontieres, but he died on arrival at the hospital. More shells have been landing in the same spot or around and we suspect they are at a tank positioned at Company Hill. A lot of damage at buildings has been caused in that area despite the low casualty figures. At 1700 hours, 21 detonations were heard by UNMOs in Potocari. We suspect they are from a multiple rocket launcher located at --" and there's a location marked, "but NCBU," which I think is "cannot be confirmed." "We cannot analyse the craters at the moment due to the continuous shelling, but we assess that the Bosnian Serb army are still using mortars, rockets, artillery and tanks." Now, on the 7th of July, I think there was bad weather, so the infantry wasn't moving on that day. Do you recall hearing all of the shell fire on that day from your position about 3.000 metres away from the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I did hear detonations occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So on the 7th of July you did, in fact, hear shelling go into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with certainty now whether it was the 6th, the 7th or the 8th. We didn't move until the 9th. We only engaged in reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move to the 8th of July, and if you can think about that particular date.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if we can have Prosecutor's Exhibit 77/8. And it's actually the fourth page of this. It's page 127. And it's just the very last paragraph, where it says, "Updates to." Your Honours, this is a report from the 8th of July, and the time indicated is 1758 hours, so it's the early evening hours of the 8th of July. "Update to: At 1354 hours DutchBat liaison officer called UNMOs and informed them of their intention to withdraw their observation post Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Foxtrot due to the heavy shelling on their positions. They said that their APC will move to a safer place as soon as shelling reduces. UNMOs had counted 60 explosions from 1335 hours to 1406 hours in Srebrenica and Potocari, and shelling is still going on. More info to come as we get it," it says in writing at the bottom of that report. Now, on that date, on the 8th of July, and I know your recollection is not that good at this time period, do you recall hearing shelling on that day? You would have heard 60 shells exploding, wouldn't you, in Srebrenica, from the position where you were located?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, until the 9th, my unit did not move from its starting position. Every day we heard occasional detonations, but these were occasional; they were not numerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now let's move to the 10th of July. And I think on the 10th of July, in the evening hours, you found yourself on the road between Zeleni Jadar and Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could just indicate to the Judges on the map. If you could put the map on the ELMO, and the usher can help you here.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we were, on the 10th in the evening, on this hill here, Bojna, above Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So let the record show that the witness has pointed to a location which is marked "Bojna." It's highlighted and it's essentially in the same grid square as the large indication of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I'm right in saying that at this point in time, Witness, you were in fact very close indeed to the town of Srebrenica, weren't you? You were, looking at this map, perhaps a matter of five hundred to a thousand metres away from the town itself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can he point on it again more closely?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Of course, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you point the location again? If you point to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would like to know how far it is exactly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you answer the Judge's question how far Bojna was from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but about 1.000 metres, one kilometre, or more.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the squares on this, I believe, Mr. McCloskey, are a kilometre, a thousand metres? I'm sorry. I put my colleague on the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: He gave us the indication. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I believe the scale of this map, it's a thousand metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Because it looks far on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'm going to read an extract from the 10th of July, and this is a report -- if you could place that on the ELMO. This is page 109. And again, I'm not going to read all of this. In the -- no. I think you've got the wrong page there, actually. At the bottom of the page, it's marked 109. Yes, that's the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the camera could come out a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Starting from the top: "Srebrenica situation update, 10 July, 1230 Bravo, July 1995. Shelling is still going on in Srebrenica. Up till now we UNMOs confirm from the morning over a hundred detonations. At 10 July 0930 hours about eight rockets were fired from grid --" and then it gives a grid reference -- "in the direction of Srebrenica." And then down to the next paragraph, which is an update on the 10th of July at 1255 hours, "Two heavy shells, probably 155-millimetre artillery shells, hit the direct surroundings of the hospital at 1100 hours. All the windows are smashed and shrapnel has showered the walls and rooms of the hospital." And the next paragraph, if the interpreters can see that, it's an update at 1346 hours on the 10th of July: "Srebrenica township is still undergoing a very heavy shelling. So far we have recorded figures 49 shells since 1250 hours to 1353 hours this afternoon with figure 9 rockets launched into the town and exchanges of occasional heavy machine-gun and small arms firing." And then the last paragraph, 1645 hours on July of 1995, and I'll just read the first two paragraphs: "Information received from one of our yellow cards who is in Srebrenica at the moment and with whom we are in contact with by radio indicates that as at 1552 hours Srebrenica town came under another heavy shelling, resulting in nine serious injuries. The western end of the town is said to be the most heavily hit, with 12 shells. It is also reported that our former location, the PTT building, is presently under a barrage of shelling, having been hit ten times in the last hour." Now, Witness, you'll agree with me that from your position at Bojna, be it 1,000 metres or 2.000 metres, you would have heard that shelling on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the position of Bojna, we reached that position in the evening hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you hear any shelling on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Cayley gave us the piece of information that in one of the squares that the distance in the squares is approximately one kilometre. I have just consulted my colleague, Mr. Petrusic. We think that this is in the ratio 1 to 50.000, which would mean that one square would be equivalent to two kilometres and not one kilometre, just by way of information and for the record, to gain a better insight of distance and impression of distance, although I am not quite certain of that. If it is -- the map is in the ratio of 1 to 50.000, that would make one square the equivalent of 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. I believe Mr. Borovcanin -- it was Mr. Borovcanin who said it was 1.000 metres. Thank you. Would you like to ask him, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We'll check the scale of the map but, frankly, 1.000 or 2.000 metres, we'll see what the witness says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So on that particular day, Witness, on the 10th of July, you don't recall hearing much in the way of shelling at your position at Bojna which was 1.000 to 2.000 metres from the centre of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We arrived at Bojna in the evening and that's why I say that on the 10th we were not at Bojna. We arrived in the evening of the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move on in time, certainly in terms of events, but it's the same day that we're talking about, which is the 10th of July, and I think you testified in your examination-in-chief that you arrived at the village of Slapovici in the morning; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th above Slapovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could take the map and place it on the projector and just indicate to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you indicate to the Judges where Slapovici is?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So for the sake of the record, the witness is indicating to the village marked Slapovici, just above the yellow sticky dot marked K, marked Kilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall, if you can, and I know it's five years ago, approximately what time you got to Slapovici on the 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was before noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you have said in your evidence that, in fact, nobody was in the village when you got there.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know where everybody was?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If for a moment, Judge Riad, we could go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Closed or private?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It's supposed to be public anyhow even if there is no one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I want to read some closed session testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Can we have private?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Private would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Private session, madam registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'm just going to read you one more piece of evidence that the Judges have heard, and this is from the commander of the Dutch forces that were in the enclave, and this is what he says occurred on the 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is, Your Honours, Colonel Karremans, whose evidence you heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: "In the southern part of the enclave, there was the so-called Swedish shelter project, a lot of housing built under Swedish authorities. In that Swedish shelter project there used to live about 3.000 refugees. As soon as the attack started in the southern part, all those refugees fled in the northern direction towards the city of Srebrenica. You can imagine there was panic, chaos in those days, what I explained before, no food. And there was no way to give them houses in Srebrenica itself. Panic I must say." Now, Witness, are you aware that the advance of the Bosnian Serb army in this area caused 3.000 to 4.000 Muslim refugees, women and children, to flee into Srebrenica? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did anybody ever speak to you about it afterwards, did anybody ever discuss that matter with you afterwards?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Slapovici?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No, I'm saying after the operation on Srebrenica, did you discuss amongst your comrades the fact that Slapovici had been empty when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't talk about it but when we got to Slapovici, Slapovici was empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did it look to you as if people had left in a hurry?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you look into any of the houses with your comrades?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was there any livestock in the village at all?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was there any sign of life at all in the village?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't notice. We just passed through. I didn't notice anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How long did you spend in the village?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only as long as it took us to pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How long was that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite a number of hour -- half an hour, half an hour to get to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you were in the village for half an hour?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the village, for as long as it took us to pass through the village, through Slapovici, and to get up on to the hill up there. About half an hour, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So it took you half an hour to pass through the village of Slapovici to Brdo?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did any of the soldiers that were with you go into any of the houses? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was in a group of 10 to 15, I don't know exactly how many of us there were. We were the reconnaissance group that moved ahead. We got to the hill and gave the sign that the army could pass through and tie up the line and, while I was there, nobody entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you were in the reconnaissance unit that was ahead of the main unit. Do you have any idea what the main unit of the Romanija Brigade actually did in Slapovici after you had left for Bojna?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When we got to the hill, we waited for the majority of forces and linked up the line and continued on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you can make no comment on what happened in the village of Slapovici after you had left with the reconnaissance unit and the main force had arrived?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do know because we waited for them up above Slapovici, some 500 metres above Slapovici, they came right behind us and we linked up the line. There was no staying behind in the village at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, let's move to the 11th of July which we've already referred to briefly when we were talking about shelling and I think in answer to some of Mr. Petrusic's questions, you said that there was artillery firing from Bojna and I think you referred to a weapon called a Browning?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Whose artillery was that? Was that Bosnian Serb artillery or was that Muslim artillery?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And where was that firing, that artillery piece, who was it firing towards?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were at Bojna, in front of us, some -- I don't know how far away, 200, 300 metres away, they had their fortification in a trench of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And they were firing at you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Towards my unit along our axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And on that occasion with this firing, how many of your unit at Bojna were killed as a result of that firing?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single man.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, let's move to the 12th of July, and let me just refresh your memory. I think in the morning you were given orders to search the terrain in the direction of Jahorina, Viogor, and Suceska; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I remember that searching of the terrain and our assembly, but I can't remember whether it was exactly on the 12th. I can't remember that and the feature and where we passed through, but we did search the terrain because our unit got the inaccessible area to search. It was a deciduous area of the forest. Now, in the 12th of the morning, we started out where Viogor, Jahorina or wherever, I don't know where we met up but the unit did assemble somewhere there. I know there was the Zvornik, the Birac and our own unit that assembled there, but I don't remember the exact spot --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you just indicate to the judges the areas where you searched where I was marked. So if you could just indicate Suceska, Jahorina and Viogora.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jahorina is there, Suceska and Viogora. But we did not go into Suceska, we were up there in the inaccessible areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So in the central area that's bordered by these three places, would that be right, this very mountainous area in the middle?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So the witness has indicated that the area that his unit was searching is the area where you can see with the very close contour lines bordered by Suceska, Jahorina and Viogora essentially in the centre of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, what exactly were you searching for up in this mountainous area?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had received the orders to move along one route axis and to come up, whether at Viogora, I'm not quite sure now, but we were following this direction and did not hit any civilians, and we moved around there. Whether there was any assembly or not, the leader was at the head.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We did not come across any civilians, the witness said, or army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you specifically said -- I'm sorry, Mr. Visnjic. Judge Riad, Mr. Visnjic wants to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Witness said, "We did not come across civilians or the army." In line 18, it just says civilians and it doesn't say the army so I just wanted to correct that. "We did not come across any civilians or members of the army." I just wanted to put that straight for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The translation is, "We did not come across any civilians," the witness said, "or army." That's what -- that was said by Mr. Cayley or by the answer. I'm looking at the transcript because it's put under "A," which is the answer. So ask witness again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, there's a little bit of confusion about what is actually in the transcript, not about what you said. Am I right in saying that you stated that, in your search, you did not come across any civilians or members of the army?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't come across any civilians or members of the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And am I right in saying that that is what you had been tasked to look for? You had been tasked to look for Muslim civilians and members of the army?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not our task to look, to search, just to pass through that axis, because I think that the units were to assemble at these three features that I mentioned. I'm not quite sure which particular feature, I can't remember that now, but we were to assemble somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What instructions were you given by your commander in the event that you did find any civilians or members of the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our duty, if a situation of that kind occurred, to hand them over. I don't know where that centre for assembly was, but we were to escort them to that particular centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you would have handed any member of the army who surrendered and, indeed, any civilian over to your commander who would have had them transferred to this centre?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move to the 12th and 13th of July when I think you stated that your unit went to its assembly point at Viogor. Do you remember saying that; are you uncertain about the date?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you just point on the map, for the benefit of the Judges, the location of Viogora?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the witness is indicating the location Viogor, which is written almost vertically down the map and it's about two squares to the left of the place marked as Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, it was at this place on either the morning of the 12th or 13th of July that you were addressed by General Mladic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General Krstic has already told the Judges in his evidence that he was present during this address by General Mladic. Do you recall seeing General Krstic when Mladic was addressing the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing anybody at all with General Mladic, any other senior officers?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot claim that I did or not. I'm not quite sure. I just know that as he addressed us. That was the first time that I saw General Mladic personally, in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he said that we should be prepared to collect our things up and move towards Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did he say anything about the success of the operation in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did he congratulate you on winning back Srebrenica for the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall if anybody, apart from General Mladic, made any kind of speech?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did Colonel Mirko Trivic speak to you at all?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody -- well I say I don't remember. I just remember that General Mladic addressed us and he told us to be prepared to move to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How long did General Mladic speak for; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not long. He just addressed us in a few words because the army was tired. The men were tired. And the doctor -- that is to say, there are a lot of tired fighters. We had not taken off our boots for about a month, and we got some skin disease because of that, so we -- the men thought they would be going home.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think on this same day, either the 12th or the 13th, after you had speech from General Mladic, you returned to Jasenovo?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you point to Jasenovo on the map? I think you'll find it's near the bottom of the map and I've marked it for you. So the witness is indicating the area marked Jasenovo directly beneath the yellow circle marked S for Sierra. Now, Witness, am I right in saying that this was the forward command post of the Romanija Brigade during the operation in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our tents were there. There were set up first of all in Zeleni Jadar when we got there, and then they were transferred to Jasenova, and that's where the army has assembled. Now, whether the command was there, well, I say again, we were given orders by our superior officer of the reconnaissance group.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing Colonel Mirko Trivic at all in Jasenova, the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 817, which is a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the photograph, in your reconnaissance unit, do you recall what communications you used, what equipment you used for communications purposes?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Motorolas.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you -- did each of you have a Motorola or was there one man who was the signaller in the unit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leader had a Motorola with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that's how he received orders from his commander?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Cayley. I was not given Exhibit 817.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can use this. It's not a very good copy, but ... If Mr. Usher could give it to the witness first. It's not a -- it's a photographic copy of a colour copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise on that photograph General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you're pointing to the man on the left of the photograph in the foreground, with a pair of binoculars. Do you recognise Colonel Mirko Trivic on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And now the witness is pointing to the gentleman on the right of the photograph, not the extreme right, who again has a set of binoculars around his neck.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've already indicated to the Judges that, in your particular unit, your commander had a Motorola and that's how he kept in contact with his superiors. Do you recall whether you saw any communications equipment in Jasenova?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So there wasn't a tent or anything at Jasenova in which you saw radio equipment?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you look at the photograph again -- you can take it off the ELMO if you wish -- and study carefully the image of Colonel Trivic. What is he holding in his left hand?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not very clear, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's a Motorola, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can assume that it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Does it look like a Motorola to you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can't see that clearly on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you place the photograph on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, for my benefit, could you -- we don't have the exhibit directly in front of us. Could you identify where the photo was taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This photograph, Your Honour, was taken in Srebrenica. This is the walk-through that was made through Srebrenica. My apologies for not -- and this is a still taken from the video that you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: As of which date?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This would be on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We'll get copies, Your Honour, of this photograph after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I was just trying to put it in time and place.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So as best you can make out, it could be a Motorola in Trivic's hand, in his left hand?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm nearly finished. Judge Riad, do you wish to take a break at this point? We've been going --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: How long do you have still?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Probably, at the most, about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'll just consult Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I think we'll continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, do you recall that after you went back to Jasenova, you then deployed with the rest of the Romanija Brigade to Zepa? Do you remember saying that on Friday?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you were unfamiliar with the route that you took from Srebrenica, from Jasenova, to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall that the route may have been via Derventa, Milici, Vlasenica, Han Pijesak and Krivaca? Do you think that's the route you may have taken?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we set off from Jasenova, I know well that the first thing I could recognise was Vlasenica, Han Pijesak, and then Plane, when we got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you do recall going through Vlasenica and Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall going through Milici?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know now. All I know is Vlasenica, Han Pijesak and Plane, as the ultimate point.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you remember that you went past the bauxite mine?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How long did it take for you to get from Jasenova to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly now. You can imagine what it is like to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. transport troops. The vehicles sometimes go out of order, there are delays. I know we got to Plane sometime in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: About what time during the day did you leave Jasenova? Now, if you think carefully, Mladic speaks to you in the morning, you return to Jasenova, you arrive at Zepa in the evening.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the afternoon, I think it was. I don't know exactly when it was that we left. All I remember well is that when we arrived at Plane, it was -- darkness was just falling, and we slept there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So if it was July and summer months, it was probably 9.00 or 10.00 in the evening when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think 8.00 or 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, did you hear Mladic's speech on the same day that you travelled from Jasenova to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember. I said it was the 12th or the 13th. I just can't remember that, what date it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think it was the 14th of July, in the morning, that you received orders to place yourself as the reserve to the Zvornik Brigade in a shop or a school in the village of Podzeplje.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think it's true that on the 15th of July you did actually replace the Zvornik Brigade, which was returning to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think, in answer to Mr. Petrusic's questions, you heard in the normal course that the reason why the Zvornik Brigade was returning to Zvornik was to deal with the Muslim fighters who were breaking out towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that later. All I know is that they were pulled out and that they had to report to the command of the Zvornik Brigade. And later I learnt that the Muslims were -- the Muslims from Srebrenica were attacking the lines under the control of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you ever hear later what happened to the Muslim fighters who had been captured during that operation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from the media, later, later.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We'll come back to that subject. Now, I think you stated that when you were at Putici you heard General Krstic on a Motorola issuing orders, I think it was to let a Muslim delegation pass. Was that your Motorola or was that your commander's Motorola?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because in my unit only the commander had a Motorola, and I was close by, next to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How did you know that it was, in fact, General Krstic on a Motorola?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognised his voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How far away were you from this Motorola?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was right next to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did General Krstic introduce himself on the Motorola?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many times prior to that had you heard General Krstic speak, prior to hearing him on the Motorola?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had heard him. He was my brigade commander from 1992 until 1994, and he spent most of his time together with us fighters on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 818. It's a new exhibit. And again, Your Honours, this is a still photograph from the video of the entrance to Srebrenica on the 11th of July. Mr. Usher, the witness can have a look at the photograph, because I think he'll be able to see it better if he studies it carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you see on that photograph General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General Krstic has a Motorola in his left hand?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you point to that Motorola? You'll need to -- I see. So could you put the pointer on there and leave it on the hand which you see holding the Motorola.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is the Motorola, in his left hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So the witness is indicating on Prosecutor's Exhibit 818 General Krstic holding a Motorola in his left hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, Witness, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honours. If I could just confer for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, have you heard of a unit called the 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of it, but I don't know anything about it. I had no occasion to meet them, nor do I know who they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Visnjic. I owe you an apology, because I have to look at them, and I don't have eyes in my back. So I apologise. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just a point of clarification regarding exhibit -- the last exhibit. Could the Prosecutor explain to us from this which exhibit was this still taken? From which video was this still taken? Has that video been shown here as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is -- I don't know the exhibit number off the top of my head, but this is the video of the entrance of General Mladic and General Krstic and their entourage into Srebrenica on the 11th of July of 1995, and we've taken a still from that particular video. I'm told it should be Exhibit number 2. I'm sorry. No, that's wrong. It's not Exhibit number 2, but I will find that in the break, the correct exhibit number, and I'll let Mr. Visnjic know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you be kind enough to provide us with that number, because we might need it for our re-examination of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I will do that in the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you said that you learned at the beginning of August that General Krstic was the new commander of the Drina Corps. From whom did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what it's like in the army. Soldiers talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you soldiers had not seen the official appointment of General Krstic, had you? You hadn't seen the documentation which made his appointment?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you wouldn't have any knowledge of the exact date of his appointment, you and your comrades; you simply weren't familiar with that information, were you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. When we returned from Zepa, we learnt that he had been appointed commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said in answer to a question put by Mr. Petrusic that Borovcanin, your last name, is a very familiar -- it's a very usual name to find in the Romanija area.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you know or had you heard of Ljubisa Borovcanin, who was the deputy commander of the Special MUP Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: He is a fairly senior officer, isn't he, within the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know he worked in MUP. Whether he was a senior officer or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is he related to you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What is your relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're relatives. We have the same patron saint. How shall I put it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think I understand it. You're cousins, essentially?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Have you ever met him?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, yes, but during the war and after it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you ever hear him referred to as "Borovcanin of the Specials," "the Specials" being the Special MUP Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, moving towards the end of my questions for you: When did you hear of the killings of Serbs by Bosniak forces in Kravica in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard later. I can't remember now all this. I learned from the media, so I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the Judges have heard in this case that upwards of 7.500 Muslim men were killed during and after the fall of Srebrenica, were killed by Bosnian Serb forces. When did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that later too from the media, whether it was on the radio or otherwise. You know, there were different figures. The Muslims were using one figure, these others another, the foreigners something else, so I heard all this from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: As your memory serves you now, how long after July of 1995 did you learn about these killings? A week, a month?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss these killings with your comrades in the Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we didn't know, our unit went along different axes and went to carry out a different task. Some people believe it, others don't believe it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And those people who do believe it, who spoke to you or you spoke with them, what did they tell you about what happened?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The story was that this had happened but we never knew what the figure was. We just couldn't understand that it could have been possible that such a thing could have happened. I don't know. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, do you believe that it took place? Do you believe that upwards of 7.500 people were murdered after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a man, I can't believe it because that is -- I don't know. I can't believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Judge Riad, I don't have any further questions for the witness so I think my learned friend may have some re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. Mr. Petrusic, would you like to ask any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President but the Defence would like to receive from the Prosecutor the exhibit from which this photograph was taken first and then, after that, we might have a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. I was planning to keep it for after the break, but you have some questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: How much time do you think you will need?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two or three questions, not many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we will resume after half an hour, at 20 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You can proceed, Mr. Cayley, but before that, we would like to make one announcement. [In French]. You have the floor, Mr. Fourmy.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Simply to inform all those present that, thanks to the efforts of the registrar, it will be possible for the Chamber to sit, as from tomorrow and until the end of the week, in courtroom number three. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that we can have another break at 1.00 for 45 minutes. That will be the lunch break, if you think that's all right. If somebody feels any emergency, especially for General Krstic, if we need to stop before that, you can please tell me. Otherwise, we will continue until 1.00. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think now the Defence have some questions to ask in re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Borovcanin, during your service in the army, did you personally use communications devices of the Motorola type?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you assert with certainty -- I'm sorry, could Exhibit 818 be placed on the ELMO first, please. Are you claiming with certainty that this is a Motorola that General Krstic is holding in his hand?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot claim that with certainty because you can't see it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour, for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Nor do I have questions. I only have to thank you, Mr. Borovcanin, for coming and for testifying and wish you a safe trip back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before the witness is taken out, there are three exhibits which I'd apply for admission, and if the witness could remain just while we do that in case there are any problems. The first exhibit is 829, which is the map of the Srebrenica enclave with the various locations identified by the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: 817 is the photograph of Colonel Trivic which the witness identified, and Prosecutor's Exhibit 818 is the photograph of General Krstic that we've just been looking at a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So I would like to apply for admission into evidence those three exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to Exhibits 818 and 817, the Defence has no objection. But regarding Exhibit 829, the Defence objects, saying that on this map which is drawn -- on which the borders are drawn in red, that those borders are not the borders of the enclave. That is our map and the red line does not indicate the borders of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, the first point that I would make, Your Honour, is it was a map that we received from the Defence so it's not a map that we produced. And in any event, the witness made absolutely no comment nor did I ask him about the boundaries of the enclave. He neither confirmed nor denied, nor do I suspect he probably knows. The purpose of the map was to indicate for your use and for greater clarity the locations that he was referring to together with the Observation Post Kilo and Sierra, so I think it can be admitted into evidence with the reservation of my learned friend, Mr. Petrusic, that indeed the red line does not accurately represent the borders of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Would that be satisfactory for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, we'll admit it into evidence with this reservation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the other ones 817 and 818.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. There was no objection about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, you can accompany the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before the next witness enters the courtroom, I should like to move into private session for a few moments to explain the protective measures that the Defence is requesting for the witness that is due to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Well, we should stop him from coming, then. Yes, we'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness DB, can you tell us in July 1995 where were you and did you receive any assignments or orders with respect to the Krivaja operation, Krivaja 95 operation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of July 1995, I was at the command post of the communications battalion at Vlasenica and I received an order to set up a communications centre at the forward command post of the Drina Corps in the Village Pribicevac region.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Who gave you that order?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember at this point in time whether the order was issued by the head of communications of the Drina Corps as the professional body who, by authorisation of the command of the Drina Corps, is empowered to issue that order or whether that order was issued personally by the Corps Commander, but I do know that I received the order in oral form.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask you to make pauses between my questions and your answers to facilitate the work of the interpreters, and also would you kindly slow down in responding to the questions, please. Was that customary, that is to say, that an order of this kind be issued orally or does it have to be given in written form?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rules and regulations applied in the army from before and the ones that apply now imply the issuance of that order in written form. However, wartime practice very often deviated from those rules and regulations and I remember that quite certainly I was issued that order orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the contents of that order, that oral order?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was an officer at that time who had been engaged in similar activities of that kind before, and I'm thinking of the war period, it was enough for me to see that from the person that -- giving me the order, conveying the order, that I was given the facts and figures where the forward command post would be, which units would be taking part in the assignment, and to be told when the communications centre of the forward command post should be completed and ready for use. That was the information I needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you get all that relevant information?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What about the units who were to take part in those combat operations?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had information as to the units to be taking part in the forthcoming operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When establishing communications at the forward command post, were these indispensable to you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For purely technical reasons that's what I needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Therefore, having received that order, you set out for the Pribicevac forward command post; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the time or, rather, the date when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The new forward command post of the Drina Corps in the village of Pribicevac, that is to say, I arrived there a day before the combat operations took place, that is to say, on the 5th of July, sometime around noon or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What did this imply, the establishment of communications or communications centre at the forward command post? Technically speaking, what did you have to do to establish the centre?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the technical sense, according to the rules that exist, it was my duty and I was assigned to establish communication between the forward command post and the superior command, that is to say, the command of the Drina Corps in Vlasenica, and to establish communication from the forward command post to the subordinate units which took part in the Krivaja 95 operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you say the "subordinate units," does that -- would you explain to that whether you mean subordinate units to the command or subordinate units who were on the terrain itself?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to the commands of the original units, their commands in the original zones, but towards the commands of the units and the units which actually took part in the Krivaja 95 operation, that is to say, those units who were grouped in the regions expecting to perform the assignments mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So this initial information, that is to say, when the corps commander or head of communications told you that there would be combat operations around Srebrenica, is that the first time you learned about that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO BOROVCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were -- that was the first information I received as to the forthcoming assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you know who issued the order for preparations for the Krivaja 95 operation?
